changes.text: Configuration drift. holzkube-manager now notices when a node's machine configuration changes behind its back (talosctl, another operator). The first time it reads a node it keeps a copy of the configuration with the secrets blacked out as that node's baseline and says so; from then on it reads every reachable node every three hours, and again after each apply it makes itself. The node page shows whether the node matches, since when it differs and the difference across all of the configuration's documents. The cluster card has a Configuration row, /metrics carries the state per node and per cluster (never 0 for a node that could not be compared), and a banner appears on every page once a drift has stood for 24 hours without being confirmed. "Confirm as intended" makes what the node has now the new baseline; it needs the admin role and the password prompt, is written to the audit log, and touches nothing on the node. There is no reset button. A node that cannot be read is never shown as matching, a damaged baseline is never overwritten, and an apply that holzkube-manager makes itself (patch, Kubernetes upgrade, CA rotation, also with a restart) is recognised as its own and does not show as drift.

What to know about it. The baseline is a plain copy on disk with the secrets blacked out, but a changed secret value alone does not show (only set versus empty), and the fields the redaction does not know (files, environment, inline manifests) are stored as the configuration view already shows them, so treat the data directory and its backups accordingly. The data directory moves to schema 7; an hourly update that rolls back to an older version will refuse it, and the guide says how to get back. Nothing here has run against a real cluster yet: that Talos returns what was sent after an apply, that it never rewrites the configuration itself, the timing after a restart (an own apply with a restart counts as its own for up to 24 hours, so a third party applying the very same bytes in that time looks like it) and the banner after real hours are all unchecked (ledger 177 to 179), and the layout and tap targets of the new parts were not seen in a browser.

Fixed: the "Cluster certificates" row added in v0.6.0 never filled in on a running manager. The read that looks at each control plane was started without a time limit, and the Talos client refuses a call that has none, so every pass failed quietly and the row stayed at "not read yet" (which is why it never said "fine" either, but also never warned). Every read now runs under its own 20 second limit. The tests missed it because each of them happened to carry a limit of its own; two new ones start the way the manager does, one of them against the simulator through the real client. Still only checked against the simulator: no real cluster has been read through it yet, so look at the row on a control plane once this is installed.

The Kubernetes upgrade chain names the newest stable patch. When a Kubernetes upgrade has to go through intermediate minors, the plan used to name each one as .0 (for example v1.33.0), which is not what anyone installs. It now asks dl.k8s.io for the newest stable patch of each minor on the way and shows that (v1.33.7, say). If that lookup fails, the plan is blocked with a sentence that says so, and never quietly falls back to .0; a target one minor away needs no lookup and is unaffected. The source has no setting. Still advice only: the job installs the version you typed in one run, so the chain tells you what to do and does not enforce it (open ledger entry 174), and a multi-minor target is blocked only while the lookup is down. Tested against the simulators and a fake server only: the format of dl.k8s.io was measured once and is not documented, and no real cluster has taken an intermediate patch from it yet (ledger 175).

The compatibility table for Talos 1.12, 1.13 and 1.14 is corrected. It allowed Kubernetes only up to 1.33, 1.34 and 1.35; Talos 1.14 supports up to 1.37, so a cluster on Talos 1.14 could not plan a chain past 1.35. The windows are now 1.30 to 1.35, 1.31 to 1.36 and 1.32 to 1.37, and the Talos 1.14 row is held against the library this build is compiled with, so it cannot fall behind again unnoticed. Older Talos rows were not re-checked.

The build pipeline uses newer GitHub Actions (checkout, setup-go, setup-node, setup-task and goreleaser, each pinned to a commit). Nothing changes in the running program; the new versions are exercised by this release's own build.

Certificate expiry inside the cluster. Until now only the certificate this manager holds itself was counted down; the ones inside the cluster ran out unseen. The cluster card now lists, under Cluster certificates, the Talos API, etcd and Kubernetes certificates and their authorities, read from every control-plane node a minute after start and then every six hours, soonest first. An authority is never renewed by Talos, so it climbs the same ladder as the admin certificate (badge at 90 days, banner on every page at 30, red at 7). A certificate Talos issues is renewed by Talos long before it runs out, so being close at all means a stuck rotation: banner at 14 days, red at 3. Until the first read the card says "not read yet", never "fine"; a control plane that does not answer keeps its last reading and the card says how many answered. The wall shows one line, only from the banner rung down, naming the certificate's role and its days and no machine, and /metrics carries holzkube_node_certificate_seconds (negative once expired). Talos keeps these certificates beside their private keys; only the name and the dates are kept here, never a key. Run against the simulator only, not yet against a real cluster.
Planning notes brought up to date and the 2026 interface mockup added to the repository (docs/mockups). Nothing changes in the running program.

Scheduled etcd backups. Per cluster you can switch on a schedule (every 6 hours, daily or weekly) and say how many to keep; each run is a job that takes the snapshot from a healthy control-plane node, skips with a stated reason when the cluster is busy, unreachable or the disk is short, and never runs twice after a restart. The Upgrades screen lists them with size and checksum, downloads one, and has a Run now button. A cluster whose last scheduled backup is more than two intervals old is marked overdue on its card and in /metrics. The backups stay on this device: they do not survive losing its SD card, so copy a download somewhere else.

Security fixes from an audit. A stolen session cookie could skip the password prompt for destructive actions just by sending any Authorization header; that is closed. Handing out a kubeconfig, talosconfig, etcd snapshot, support bundle or pod log is now written to the audit log (the kubeconfig was documented as audited and was not). "Host: localhost" from another machine no longer reaches the password routes of an address that is single-sign-on only. Password hashing runs two at a time, so a burst of logins cannot exhaust the Pi's memory; anonymous requests that write to the audit log or create sessions are limited per address; expired sessions are swept while running; failed sign-ins and the peer address now appear in the journal.

The updater is stricter. It installs only a newer version (a downgrade needs --allow-downgrade), picks the highest release rather than the first listed, refuses a release without checksums.txt, remembers a version that failed its health check instead of retrying it every hour, replaces the program and itself atomically, and wants three healthy answers in a row before it calls an update good. --rollback now takes the lock and records itself. Releases are cut only from main, and CI actions are pinned and scanned for known vulnerabilities.

Removing a node is now a job. It leaves etcd, waits for it to settle, wipes the system disk and forgets the node, resumes after a restart, holds the cluster's lease and is shown step by step; the refusals (quorum, wrong cluster) stay immediate. The quorum check counts the voters that actually answer, not the ones on record. The route answers 202 with the job instead of 200, which matters only to scripts that call it.

Fixes. Cancelling a running job ends it as cancelled instead of leaving it running and resuming after a restart; staged configuration can be applied again after the node rebooted; streams, forgotten machines and finished jobs no longer leak goroutines and memory. In the interface, one failed session check no longer throws you to the login page, log panels no longer repeat lines, the upgrade plan resets when you change the target, error messages are announced to screen readers, and dates use one format.

A button on the Upgrades screen asks whether there is a newer Talos: it compares what your nodes report with the newest stable release this version can install, names the next run (Talos goes one minor at a time) and links the release notes. The dashboard shows a badge on a cluster that has an update. Asking changes nothing and reads no node.

A Talos upgrade now needs a fresh etcd snapshot of the cluster, taken here, before it can be confirmed or started. The snapshot is taken from the Upgrades screen, kept on this machine (not in backups, the newest two per cluster) and counts for an hour. The server enforces it, not only the screen. Kubernetes upgrades are unchanged.

The interface uses its space better. On a wide screen Settings, Config and Jobs sit in two columns and Nodes is a card; on a tablet the dashboard's clusters and recent activity sit side by side; a cluster's downloads and actions are one row each instead of a column of buttons; and on a phone a table row is a card with its values two to a line, about half as tall.

Security and updates: the library behind running a command in a container (spdystream) and golang.org/x/crypto are raised for published denial-of-service and security fixes, along with grpc, go-jose and a few smaller ones. Taking a safety snapshot is now one at a time per cluster, cut off after 30 minutes, refuses a cluster that does not exist without leaving anything behind, and no longer names a data-directory path in its refusals.

Talos machinery is raised from v1.14.0 to v1.14.2, the newest stable release, so the configuration documents of a v1.14.2 cluster are read by the library this product carries. The supported range stays v1.14.

Fixed the redesign's navigation and dashboard. On a wide screen there is one navigation again, the labelled list; the icon rail only stands in for it on a tablet. The dashboard now uses the whole screen: the three fact cards on top, below them the machines (host, state, role, address, Talos version) and, beside them, every cluster with its nodes and certificate and the latest audit records.
On a phone the three fact cards sit in one row, and the Kubernetes sections are one row that scrolls sideways (the open one stays in view) instead of three rows.

The interface is the 2026 redesign: on a desk and a tablet the navigation is an icon rail (Dashboard, Clusters, Host, Jobs, Settings) with the full list as a labelled column beside it, on a phone the five sit as a bottom tab bar with icons and labels. The dashboard shows the fleet as cards with one big number each -- clusters, machines, the instance's own state -- instead of stacked reports. Logo, colours and every rule the shell carries (the Host mark, the audit chain warning, the 44px phone targets) are unchanged.
Fixed: the navigation's name and tagline fit on one line each. The bar is a little wider (240 px); the tagline had broken onto two lines and the name could run past the edge.
Releases are built for the Raspberry Pi 5 only for now (linux/arm64). The archives for amd64, macOS and Windows are gone, for the daemon and for holzkubectl; a Pi updating itself notices nothing.

The interface takes the new brand colour. The accent is Glut instead of brass: buttons, the selected navigation entry, focus rings, the Alpha badge and the first line of every chart. In the light theme, text and borders in that colour use a darker Glut, so they keep the contrast they had. Nothing else changes.

New Host page: the machine holzkube-manager runs on — device, service, live CPU, memory, filesystems, temperatures and network, with history over 1 h, 6 h and 24 h, a warning that names its reason, and a tile on the wall. What the service's hardening hides is shown as "not readable", never as 0.

Five host actions on /host: check for updates (installs nothing), check for updates and install, restart the service, restart the host, shut it down. Each needs the operator role, a fresh re-authentication and the typed host name, and is in the audit log. holzkube-manager never does them itself: a small root-owned helper from deploy/ carries them out, and the page says what to install while it is missing or too old.

The hourly update now ships as units in deploy/ (holzkube-manager-update.service and .timer, plus a unit for the daemon itself). The update script checks the host before it installs, rolls back when the restart fails, and never runs twice at once. Your hand-made units keep working; deploy/HOST-HELPER.md says how to switch to the shipped ones.
On a phone every control is at least 44 px, also inside menus and dialogs; the build fails when one is smaller. Nothing changes above tablet width.

Settings → Accounts can unlink an account from single sign-on, so you can move to another identity provider. Unlinking ends the sessions that came in through that link; the next single sign-on from the local network links the new provider and is recorded in the audit log. Service accounts no longer block linking, and an address that only accepts single sign-on no longer answers "setup required" when there is more than one account.

Not yet run on real hardware: the host helper, the shipped update units under their sandbox, and the phone hand test. Install the helper per deploy/HOST-HELPER.md and start with Check for updates, which changes nothing.

Kubernetes upgrades rebuilt. The upgrade now runs in the order talosctl upgrade-k8s uses: it pulls every image onto every node first, then moves kube-apiserver, kube-controller-manager and kube-scheduler node by node, waiting until each node reports the pod ready on its new image, then kube-proxy (its DaemonSet included, with a rollout wait), and the kubelets last.

Fixed: a Kubernetes upgrade would have replaced a node's whole configuration with its few image lines, and a real node refuses that, so every run would have stopped at its first node. Each change now merges into the configuration the node has, in the shape it keeps it (Talos v1.14 documents or the older fields).
The Kubernetes upgrade is tested end to end against the simulator, not yet against a real cluster. Take an etcd snapshot before you run it.
The update script finds prerelease builds and, after a healthy update, replaces itself from the release archive. A host running the script from before v0.0.1 needs the new one installed once by hand.

A fresh start at 0.0.1. holzkube-manager is alpha software under heavy development: any release can change or break features, the API and the data directory's format. Keep a backup of the data directory and read these notes before updating. Everything below is what this first alpha already does.

Clusters and nodes: adopt an existing Talos cluster from its talosconfig or provision a new one. The manager follows the cluster's own membership, so a node that joins or leaves shows up by itself, and every page reads live from the cluster when you open it.
Live hardware per node: load overall and per core, memory, disks, network, temperatures and fans, with the last 24 hours kept across restarts.
Apps: everything that runs on Kubernetes, grouped by what was installed, with its CPU and memory now and over the day, and a page per app with its pods, services and events.
Kubernetes: workloads, pods and why one is broken, events, storage, networking, quotas, who may do what, cordon and drain, applying a manifest and running a command in a container.
Power for a cluster, a node or an app: stop, force stop, start, disable, enable, restart and force restart. Start wakes a switched-off node by Wake-on-LAN.
Talos upgrades built from Image Factory schematics, SecureBoot, disk encryption, etcd snapshots and restore, and certificate renewal.
A wall for a screen in the office: every node and workload as a tile, how full the cluster is, the day's load and the latest warnings.

A local account and single sign-on, roles, a password prompt before anything destructive, a hash-chained audit log and a dry-run mode. holzkubectl on the command line, Prometheus metrics and a support bundle.
A mark of its own: annual rings in a hexagon, as the tab icon, in the sidebar and on a phone's home screen.
